posts.content_md:
Hey Joe, I thought I would post here as I already have enough group logons and didn't want to sign up with google also.

When I was using a fringe locker I noticed a couple of things.

If your fringe movement (amplitude) in the short time is larger then the movement range of your piezo then you will not get a good lock. The electronics can minimize that with "jumps" to the correct same relative position but the speed at which the electronic can react will dictate fringe contrast.

If your fringe drift is larger then the movement range fo your piezo but is very slow, you will get a good lock that will jump once in a while. This isn't so bad and will give you a hologram but depending on how able the fringle locker is to bring the fringes back to the same spot after the jump will determine the contrast of your fringes. This too can be controlled with the elctronics.

Third and most important. If you have movement in your fringes without the fringe locker then the chances are that you will have the same movement after the copy hologram and totally within the fringe locker. This gives a false reading to the locker and may move the piezo to compensate for movement in the michaelson after the hologram and thus ruin the hologram on purpose. It is most important that the everthing be as stable as possible and for sure the fringe locker michaelson be the most stable items on the table. 

It would not even be a bad idea to lock down the michaelson set up for the locker with heavy weights, glue and clamps (if you get my point).

Our exposures were 30 to 45 minutes. I would watch the finges without the fringe locker turned on for 30 to 45 minutes and make sure they did not move more then one fringe for that duration. If they did, it was back to securing and locking down optics even better. Once I was within the 1 fringe movement I would turn on the fringe locker. The fringes would stay completely locked for the duration of the exposure in resist.

posts.content_md:
Thanks for your comments, John. Yes, obviously if the transducer can't handle the path length differential, the darn thing will lose its lock. And of course, the setup should already be as stable as possible, since fringe-locking is not a cure-all, but best suited to correcting slow fringe drift.

A photoresist holographer with many years of experience told me that he often locks his setup down in the evening, then comes back the next morning with it still locked in place. That says something about the potential of fringe-locking. His circuit was homemade, and it sounded pretty primitive. What I'm interested in is making a good fringe-locker from available components, not using a commercially-made fringe-locker. I want to know specifically what op-amps are good, how the differential circuit should be layed out, what kinds of photodetectors work well (photodiode or phototransistor, bare or fiber-coupled), specifically what kind of transducers are good (speaker coils, piezo stacks), etc. All this is with the intention of building a good (even excellent) fringe-locker for about $100.

> **JohnFP:** Joe, I have one that I commissioned an electronic engineer I know to build. Will pics alone work and I might be able to answer any specific questions on the components?

Thanks a lot, John. I would like to know more about your fringe-locker. The most helpful thing would be a schematic diagram of the circuit, but maybe you don't have that. It might be pretty difficult to deduce anything significant from photos. Even if I could see the circuit in person, it might not be possible to identify all the components. Some good close-up photos of the circuit board might be interesting, though.

I'm also interested in the type of operational amplifier chip, assuming it uses one. This will possibly be an 8-pin chip. I used the 741, which is very common, but I think its performance is limited (so I'm looking into a replacement).

I am also uncertain as to what type of transducer is best. Speaker coils are common, as are so-called "bimorphs" (specified in the Stabilock). Bimorphs, as far as I can tell, are just another name for piezo stacks, and they are driven with higher voltages than speaker coils. This complicates the circuit (and they are more expensive), so I would prefer to use a speaker coil. Someone on the sci.electronics.design forum said that bass speakers can travel 10mm which of course would be super-adequate (though I don't know if they will be otherwise suitable).

Since I'm basically a tinkerer when it comes to electronics, anything built by a professional would be interesting to me, so if you have any technical information about your fringe-locker, John, I would appreciate knowing about it. I would also like to compensate you for your time.

posts.author: Joe Farina
posts.content_md:
> **Colin Kaminski:** Do you find that 10mm is useful?

No. I mentioned it because it's interesting: one limitation of fringe-locker transducers has been considered to be lack of sufficient movement (I think this has happened to me with the small speaker I used, in conjunction with a low-power operational amplifier.) Piezo stacks have been vaunted as superior to speakers, but I think the following facts should be borne in mind: the Thorlabs piezo actuator stack that has the most dispalcement moves 15 microns (that should be more than enough for a fringe-locker), but the price is $99 and it requires 100 volts. As far as movement is concerned, a speaker coil can obviously outstrip it (by a huge margin, supposedly about 10mm), it's easier to implement because it doesn't require high voltage, and it's much cheaper.

posts.author: Joe Farina
posts.content_md:
Thanks, John. I mentioned the movement potential of speaker coils because I thought it was interesting. Of course, you are right, this large movement is not needed for fringe-locking. Even 5 microns is probably quite sufficient, and I think this is what's specified as the maximum for the Stabilock II.

I've been making some good progress with fringe-locker research, and have ordered a number of components for testing, such as a variety of different op-amps, photodiodes, phototransistors, precision resistors, small speakers, etc. I've found a circuit that can drive high-voltage, but it needs to be modified to incorporate a differential amplifier. Then I can test one of the Thorlabs piezo transducers which (may?) have better angular stability (i.e., won't twist as much as a mirror glued to the center of a speaker membrane). Speaker coils "float" around the magnets, and they are only attached to the membranes. It seems that the mirror would need to be glued to this thin membrane. I'm a bit concerned that this arrangement may result in unwanted angular deflection when it moves back and forth. Supposedly, piezo stacks also suffer from angular displacement, but they might be better than speakers.

I've found an inexpensive source for high voltage DC to DC (e.g. 5V to 100V) converters at [http://www.emcohighvoltage.com](http://www.emcohighvoltage.com) But I still need to figure out how to incorporate this into a differential amplifier circuit.

I was really surprised to find out that a university course-project on fringe-locking is actually being taught this fall at the University of Arizona, taught by a well-known figure in holography, Dr. Raymond K. Kostuk. I sent him an e-mail, hopefully he will respond.

posts.content_md:
Ahhh..hahaha. That's too funny.

This is interesting. It seems your fringe locker should be placed such that each photo cell is half way between a light and dark fringe and on opposite side of the fringes such that a movement in the fringes one way and photo cell 1 gets more light as photo cell 2 gets less light and if the fringes move the other way photo cell 1 get less light and photo cell 2 gets more light.

In a fringe locker with the cells in series, each photo cell should be placed half way between a light and dark fringe but they should be on the same side of the fringe such that a movement in one way gives both cells more light and a movement in the other way gives both cells less light. 

Does this logic sound correct?

With mine, I line up the photocells as described and then adjust the pot both ways finding the maximum movement each way of the Piezo. Then I adjust the pot half way between these extreems. This give a nice ballance and allows the most movement in both directions.

Also, the size of the fringe is important. I would have to say the larger the fringe is the higher the resolution of the fringe locker. My photo cells are almost a inch in separation. I try to place the photo cells one fringe apart.

I tried many times to try to steal light directly from the overflow of the reference and object beams with a single beam splitter such that a full michaelson did not need to be constructed but found it very difficult to do.

Yes, in my design, I found that a good position is on either side of a bright fringe. The design of your fringe locker (as shown on your website) may be different. Do you think both of your detectors are connected in series? If so, that's a real brain twister. Obviously your locker works well. I'm gonna have to think agout that one. Also, the detectors appear to be located on the circuit board itself. So you put the whole circuit board into the fringes?

The main part of your system appears to be the Burr-Brown INA114 which is a (now discontinued) precision op-amp. The thing which distinguished that chip was its very low offset voltage, but newer chips have even better performance. It's interesting that your engineer chose that chip, perhaps because of this factor. I had the feeling that low offset voltage is important in this application, so maybe this is confirmed by the presence of the INA114. Another IC in your design, the 7660, appears to be a voltage converter, and I don't know why it was included. The third IC must be very outdated, as there is no kind of description when that part number is Googled. Judging by your drawing, the piezo looks like an ordinary piezo speaker. When I built my fringe-locker, I tried using a piezo speaker first, but it didn't work. When I tried magnet-coil speakers, they did. I'm going to try another piezo speaker when my parts come in.

When using a piezo with a limited movement range, it may be necessary to center the travel as you describe. I haven't tried to do this myself yet, I just tweak the gain and damping potentiometers until the fringes are locked. I'm a bit curious about the procedure you mentioned. How do you know when the piezo is centered correctly?

I agree about the large fringes. Also, it's been said that horizontal fringes are better than vertical ones, since table movement is generally in the up-and-down direction rather than side-to-side.

That's interesting about the difficulty in taking light directly from the overspill for the object and reference beams. I was looking at some of the drawings in the second edition of Saxby regarding this. I was having some trouble in figuring out the correct procedure as desribed by Saxby for the reflection scenario. This involves a mirror (instead of a beamsplitter used in a transmission setup), but the geometry looked rather odd. I would like to see if I can generate some fringes like he described. It would be simpler than using a separate Michelson as you descibed (which is the way I planned to do it originally).

In the last 20 years or so, there has been another method used by a group in Brazil which takes advantage of real-time effects in resists. Moire fringes are generated from the newly-forming hologram itself (no secondary holograms or interferometer fringes are involved). But the recording material needs to have at least a very weak real-time effect. I asked one of the researchers about the potential for using this technique with DCG, and he thought it would work (and so do I).

posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md:
> **Joe:** Do you think both of your detectors are connected in series?

Well, in looking at diagram 2 I see a wire that connects one of the ends of each of the photo cells. It is the leftmost central red wire. I am not real good at electronics so maybe I am reading it wrong. Maybe your expertise can tell me if I am correct or not.

> **Joe:** Also, the detectors appear to be located on the circuit board itself. So you put the whole circuit board into the fringes?

Actually yes. I take a white card and cover the entire board with exception of two holes cut out, one for each photo cell. This allows me to see pretty precisely where the fringes are in relation to the cells. The photo cell is smaller then its mount. So my holes are just big enough to open where the inner part (the actual cell) is.

> **Joe:** Judging by your drawing, the piezo looks like an ordinary piezo speaker.
 Yes it is. It is one I took out of a smoke detector. It is important to have the mirror smaller then the white crystal part of the piezo. It is also important to remember how the piezo wants to move. It is a disk that will want to bend into a convex or concave bowl form. So with that it is also important to glue the mirror with just a single small drop of glue in the very center of the piezo white crystal part. Then to mount the crystal's back to a gimbal mount, I do the following. I take a flat metal washer in which the inner diameter is just slightly smaller then the outer most diameter of the whole disk. I put two very small drops of epoxy very close to one another on the inside edge of the washer. I then put two more drops very close together on the opposite side of the inner washer edge. This allows the disk to cup in or bow out in the center thus moving the mirror in and out. If you glue the entire back of the piezo to a flat base the piezo is restricted in it concaving and convexing movement. I hope I explained this clearly. If you look at a standard cone speaker you will notice the cone is supported by the outer ring only which allows the center part an in and out motion.

> **Joe:** How do you know when the piezo is centered correctly?

I turn the piezo on and move the set of photo cells until the fringes seem locked. If you then turn the pot very, very slowly one way you should see the fringes move in a direction. At some point the fringe either stops moving or the fringes jump to the next set of fringes. Either of these is the max in that direction. The same can be done the other way. Then adjust in the middle.

> **Joe:** Also, it's been said that horizontal fringes are better than vertical ones, since table movement is generally in the up-and-down direction rather than side-to-side.

I have never heard of that one. If your mirrors are perfectly perpendicular to the table and you get an up and down motion, there would be no change in path lengths of the mirrors. What we are trying to control here is very simply a change in the relative path lengths of the two beams. If you set up a Michelson and get a bulls eye pattern then introduce any type of motion the horizontal and vertical parts of the bulls eye fringes move exactly the same distance. So if you only look at (or set your photo cells at) the horizontal or verticals fringes you should see the same relative movement in my opinion.

I am not sure I have the Saxby second edition. I will have to look. I do have the third edition and don't recall a mention of fringe locking.

I see.

As to the question of up-and-down table movement, what I really should have said was slow, irregular table warpage, not "movement." This warpage would cause path length changes. I got the impression from the person I talked to that this would cause more fringe movement when horizontal fringes are used instead of vertical.

As soon as my lab is ready, I would like to test this theory by setting up a Michelson, then displacing the two dots vertically, then expanding them (to produce horizontal fringes), then counting the number of fringes which drift over a given time period. Then displace the dots horizontally (to make vertical fringes) and do the same. It should be an easy way to test this idea.

But perhaps the best thing to do is generate circular fringes, as you suggested. I guess all types of movement would be apparent with circular fringes, but I've never used them and they don't seem to appear in the Michelson arrangement. I think circular fringes appear in the Mach-Zehnder interferometer with careful alignment, according to Saxby.

If you don't have the second edition of Practical Holography, I will send you Appendix 5: Fringe Stabilization. This is 8 pages long and is pretty substantial (I think it's worth reading). It shows some geometries similar to the ones you posted. But as you mentioned, I can see how the "light spillover" method might generate some very weak fringes.

I forgot to mention something regarding horizontal fringes. The two commercially-made lockers that I know of, the Stabilock II and the one made by a company in Michigan called Data Optics, use two detectors which are displaced vertically. On the Stabilock website, if the picture showing the detector head is printed on paper (it's more difficult to see on a computer monitor in my case) then it's pretty clear that the two holes are displaced vertically. So this suggests that the detector arrangement assumes horizontal fringes.

Must be artistic license. The detector head can be oriented in any direction to fit your fringes.

I was reading the first edition of Saxby (I hadn't seen this in a long time), and noticed a couple of references to fringe-locking literature which I don't have. The first paper was by Nick Phillips, and was in the second International Symposium on Display Holography (1985), pages 111-30. If anyone has this paper, I would be happy to buy it or trade for it.

Based on Saxby's comments, Rallison appears to have created a company called International Dikrotek to market his fringe-locker, called the DK-10. "International Dikrotek" sounded like an odd name, and after a while I got the joke. It also made me wonder why Rallison chose the "con" suffix for Ralcon.

> **Joe:** ...Piezo stacks have been vaunted as superior to speakers, but I think the following facts should be borne in mind: the Thorlabs piezo actuator stack that has the most dispalcement moves 15 microns (that should be more than enough for a fringe-locker), but the price is $99 and it requires 100 volts.....

[http://cgi.ebay.de/Laser-Spiegel-mit-Pi ... dZViewItem](http://cgi.ebay.de/Laser-Spiegel-mit-Piezo-Ansteuerung-Laserspiegel_W0QQitemZ110025764052QQihZ001QQcategoryZ12469QQcmdZViewItem)

or

[http://cgi.ebay.de/Laser-Spiegel-mit-Pi ... dZViewItem](http://cgi.ebay.de/Laser-Spiegel-mit-Piezo-Ansteuerung-Laserspiegel_W0QQitemZ110025764052QQihZ001QQcategoryZ12469QQcmdZViewItem)

This item contains a piezo stack, about 10 x 4 x 3 mm.

I have bought some of them, took one apart and tested the piezo stack.

It expands /contracts 633 nm (2 fringes) every 18 Volts.

Suitable for Fringe Locking or for a Scanning Fabry-Perot Interferometer.

There is also a first surface mirror there, it's reflectivity is about 93% @633nm.

posts.author: Joe Farina
posts.content_md:
Thanks for the links.

For the time being, I'm going to try low-voltage speakers (magnetic or piezo). I used to think that high-voltage piezo stacks had less out-of-plane movement (less deflection) but now I'm not so sure:

[http://departments.colgate.edu/physics/ ... driver.htm](http://departments.colgate.edu/physics/research/Photon/root/Apparatus/piezo_driver.htm)

To quote: "We scan the position of one of the mirrors of the interferometer by putting a piezo-electric stack (Thorlabs AE0505D08 - $129) as an insert in a translation stage. It works better than mounting the mirror on the piezo, because the piezo moves slightly in two dimensions, introducing a misalignment as it is scanned."

I've been thinking about another application for piezo-stacks, though. I wonder if anyone has tried to build a spatial filter using piezos to fine-tune the movement?

I may have a problem in the future when I try to put my beams through a 2 or 5 micron pinhole, with the lasers completely off the table (I need those small pinholes because some of my setups require a highly diverging reference beam). So alignment may become a real pain. I wonder if it's feasible to use piezos as part of a spatial filter (maybe inserted in front of the main screws in a commercial unit, or as part of a homemade one). Then the table would not need to be touched for fine tuning, because it would be done electronically (?)

posts.author: Colin Kaminski
posts.content_md: This is a great idea. I think and automated spatial filter alignment mechenism could easily be created with a couple of servos and a PID.

posts.author: geso
posts.content_md:
"I've been thinking about another application for piezo-stacks, though. I wonder if anyone has tried to build a spatial filter using piezos to fine-tune the movement? "

I did this with a surplus fiber launcher, called a FiberLine Launchmaster, and an objective lens on a small translating mount. I attached a pinhole where the original lens was. I bought this off ebay(of course) thinking the driver was for piezo elements, but instead it uses electro-magnetic coils to control movement. Fun to play with, but for the most part sits dormant with all the other stuff...
